segments.text: Chapter 2. The Big News
The village square hummed with morning.
A baker slid a tray of pão de queijo into a window, and the warm, cheesy smell drifted past the cobblestones.
Aranha walked with Teia on his shoulder, her tiny blue legs tickling his neck.
He waved to a capybara sweeping the step of the corner shop.
A flash of color dropped from the sky.
Toco the toucan landed on the lamppost with a clatter of claws, his orange beak catching the sun like a slice of mango.
He flapped his black-and-white wings and chirped, "Aranha!
Aranha!
I have the news!"
Aranha’s eight hands stilled.
"What news, Toco?"
"The big match!
Today!
The Jungle Spiders against the Jaguars!"
Toco bobbed his head, and the rolled-up newspaper in his beak wobbled.
"Everyone in the village will be there—monkeys, coatis, even the sloth who sleeps through everything!"
Aranha’s tummy did a little flip.
The Jaguars were fast, with paws that pounded the grass and tails that swished like whips.
He had seen them score goal after goal.
A flutter started in his chest, light as a moth.
Teia nudged his cheek with her head.
Aranha took a breath and looked at Toco.
"I’ll do my best," he said, and the words came out steadier than he expected.
Toco tilted his head, his beak a bright grin.
"We know you will!
The whole village will be cheering your name!"
He launched from the lamppost, wings beating a happy rhythm as he soared toward the field.
Aranha watched him go.
The flutter was still there, but now it felt like the buzz before a kickoff.
He turned toward the field, Teia clinging to his collar, ready to warm up.
At the edge of the field, Aranha found an open space.
He set the ball down and took a step back.
“Okay, Teia,” he said.
“Let’s see what we can do.”
He raised one hand and focused.
From his wrist, a thin, silvery strand shot out—thwip!
It stuck to the ball.
He pulled, and the ball wobbled toward him.
A little wobbly, but it came.
He tried again.
Thwip!
This time, he caught it with two hands.
Then he gave the web a gentle swing, and the ball arced through the air.
He imagined it sailing past a goalie, into a net.
Teia bounced on the grass, her tiny legs a blur.
She seemed to say, “You can do it!”
Aranha practiced over and over.
Sometimes the ball spun away.
Sometimes it plopped at his feet.
But each time, he learned a little more.
His webs weren’t just for climbing—they could be part of the game.
“Maybe this will help us today,” he said.
He tucked the ball under one arm and jogged toward the field, where the stands were already filling with animals.
